criteria: WHEN a registered key signs the challenge, THE server SHALL mint a session token that works on /rpc
WHEN a challenge is reused or expired, THE login SHALL be refused
WHEN the session token expires, THE next CLI call SHALL log in again without human action
WHEN ssh-keygen is unavailable or the key is agent-only, THE refusal SHALL say so in one sentence
WHEN the legacy invite-token flow is used, THE behaviour SHALL be unchanged
card.spec:
THE DECISION THIS CARD IMPLEMENTS, chosen over per-request signing: a key authenticates a LOGIN, and the login mints a short-lived SESSION TOKEN through the `store/creds.py` machinery that already exists. Every downstream path — /rpc bearer auth, /feed, the MCP board — is UNTOUCHED. Signing every request would mean teaching the stdlib HTTP server, the WebSocket handshake and the MCP layer a signature envelope each; the session model changes exactly one thing: where tokens COME FROM. They stop being things a human copies and become artifacts a key mints.

THE MECHANISM is OpenSSH's own, the same one git commit signing uses:

  client:  ssh-keygen -Y sign  -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -n taskops  <payload>
  server:  ssh-keygen -Y verify -f <root>/allowed_signers -I <principal> -n taskops

The signed payload is a server-issued CHALLENGE: client POSTs /login {principal}, server answers a random nonce + expiry (single-use, short TTL, kept in memory), client signs it, POSTs the signature, server verifies against allowed_signers and mints a token with a TTL. A challenge, not a client timestamp — no clock-skew window to reason about, no replay cache to size; the nonce dies on use.

SUBPROCESS: `ssh-keygen` runs via a new `gitwork/sig.py` routed through `gitwork/run.py` — the one module allowed subprocess, and the architecture test keeps enforcing exactly that. Client-side signing lives there too. NO pip dependency, NO hand-rolled crypto: if ssh-keygen is absent the refusal says so and names the package.

CLI: `taskops host add <name> <url>` records a host alias + which key to use (default ~/.ssh/id_ed25519). `board.py::open_board` learns to refresh: when the stored session token is expired/absent and the config names a host with a key, log in transparently and cache the new token where remote.json lives today. A human never copies a token again; `remote.json` becomes a session cache, refreshable, deletable.

INVITES BECOME KEY REGISTRATION: `taskops join <url>?invite=…` sends the invite AND the user's pubkey; the server burns the invite, registers the key as a member principal, and the first login proceeds keyed. The old flow (invite mints a standing bearer token) KEEPS WORKING — rule 3 — and the docstring marks it as the legacy path.

KNOWN LIMIT, stated not solved: `ssh-keygen -Y sign` wants the private key FILE; ssh-agent-only setups (no key file on disk) cannot sign yet. Refuse with a sentence naming the limit. Do not build agent-protocol support in this card.

Tests: full login round-trip over real HTTP (generate a throwaway keypair in the test, register it, challenge, sign, verify, minted token calls a verb); a wrong key fails; a reused challenge fails; an expired challenge fails. Mutation-check one site at a time.

The scp dies. One command turns this repo's local board into the hosted one:

THE ORDER IS THE SAFETY, config flips LAST:

GitHub's visibility model, deliberately and exactly: a board is PRIVATE by default; the owner may mark it PUBLIC; public means ANONYMOUS READ; write requires a registered key — always, with no third state and no anonymous-write grace.

THE FLAG is a project-level event (`verbs/project.py`, where `remote` already lives), set through a server-scope verb, owner only: `taskops board visibility <host>/<name> public|private`. Derived into the board payload so the UI can say it; OPTIONAL key in types.ts with its @source line.

And READS MUST STOP WRITING for that actor: every read verb opens with `stores.live.renew(actor, now)` — presence, a WRITE to live.sqlite. FOUND BY RUNNING THE WHOLE FLOW END TO END, not by a test: a freshly bootstrapped owner CANNOT CREATE THEIR FIRST BOARD from the laptop. Reproduced verbatim on a clean host:

    $ taskops server init --root srv --key key.pub --owner berna      # ok
    $ taskops board create http://host/e2e --key ./key
    taskops: no session for http://host — join it with a key first:
             taskops join <url>?invite=… --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

DEADLOCK: the invite that join needs is minted by `taskops invite` — which also wants a session — and there is no board to join yet anyway. The owner's only way in today is the break-glass `--root` on the box, i.e. THE SSH ANOMALY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS TO KILL, on day one of every host.

THE CAUSE, precisely: `cli/operate.py::call()` obtains a token ONLY from `session.fresh(root, config)`, which needs the `login{host, principal, key}` block a previous `join --key` or `board push --key` wrote into `remote.json`. `cli/push.py::_session()` already solved this exact problem — given `--key` it signs in directly, deriving the principal from the config's login block or from `commands.actor()` — but that solution lives INSIDE push and the other five verbs cannot reach it.

Proof the server side is fine: `session.sign_in(root, host, 'berna', key)` + `board.create` over the wire works first try; after ONE keyed call writes the login block, every operate verb works with no flags. The gap is only the FIRST command in a fresh checkout.

THE FIX — extraction, not invention:
1. LIFT push's key-to-session logic out of `cli/push.py::_session` into `session.py` (something like `session.establish(root, host, config, key=…, principal=…)`): with a key → sign in directly and cache the login block; without → `session.fresh` as today; neither → the existing refusal, which should now ALSO name `--key` as the way in (today it only names join, which is wrong for the owner).
2. `--key <path>` (and `--as <principal>`, defaulting to the login block else `commands.actor()`'s name — the $USER guess must be overridable: today a machine whose unix user differs from the principal cannot sign in at all) accepted by ALL of `board create`, `board ls`, `board visibility`, `invite`, `revoke`. `push.py` then consumes the same helper — one implementation, two callers, no drift.
3. After any successful keyed call, the login block is cached exactly as push does it — so the SECOND command needs no flags, which the e2e proved is already the pleasant steady state.

Test, in `tests/test_topology.py`, the exact scenario that failed: fresh host, `server init`, then `taskops board create --key` AS THE FIRST EVER COMMAND from a checkout that never joined — through the real CLI entry point (`main()`), not by calling the functions, because the wiring is what was broken (this chapter already learned that lesson: the `upstream=` mutation that stayed green because every test built the server directly). card.spec:
THE HUMAN'S OWN WORDS, and they are the spec: «esto debería ser como git — `taskops remote add https://host/` · `taskops board create taskops-v2` · `taskops board push` — pero sin --key». Today every operate verb wants the full URL and a `--key` flag; git asks for neither, and the reasons it does not are both mechanisms we can copy exactly.

1. **`taskops remote add <url>`** — records the host FOR THIS CHECKOUT, like `git remote add` records origin per clone. It writes the `login.host` block in `remote.json` (the private, per-machine file — exactly where `join --key` and `push --key` already cache it; git's remotes live in `.git/config`, also uncommitted). It does NOT sign in — recording an address is not an act of identity — but it validates the shape and says what to do next. `taskops remote` with no args prints it, `git remote -v` style. This does NOT contradict operate.py's no-alias-registry docstring and the docstring must say why: an alias TABLE (many names, global) was refused; ONE host per checkout in the file that already holds it is the same fact `join` records, acquired earlier.

2. **KEY DISCOVERY, ssh's own**: when no `--key` is given and no login block names one, try `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.ssh/id_ecdsa`, `~/.ssh/id_rsa` — the identity files ssh itself tries, in that order — and use the first that exists. The refusal when NONE exists lists what was tried and names `--key`. `--key` stays as the override, exactly like `ssh -i`. Discovery lives in ONE function in `session.py` beside `establish()`, and `establish()` consumes it — not six call sites each guessing.

      your own worktree first:
        cd /Users/berna/taskops-v2/.taskops/trees/tk-a1b7f2 && git merge ms/actors-…
      then taskops_merge task=tk-a1b7f2 again

Every single time, the human's next act was to execute those two lines unchanged and call `taskops_merge` again. When the diagnosis AND the remedy are both the board's, and the remedy is mechanical, refusing is not safety — it is toil. Its own docstring already knows the half of it: "This session paid six round trips to that."

WHY THE REFUSAL EXISTED, so the fix does not un-learn it: the alternative was merging a stale branch and getting a CONFLICT ABOUT A FILE with the real cause ("this branch never pulled the chapter in") nowhere in the message. The refusal named the cause. The fix must keep naming it — and go one step further when the step is safe.

THE FIX, in `gitmoves.py::merge` where `_refuse_if_stale` is called today (between the `state != "done"` check and `trees.merge_card`):

1. `trees.behind(repo, branch, card_branch)` says the card is behind (that function — `gitwork/trees.py::behind` — is one `merge-base --is-ancestor` plus a `rev-list --count`; it does not change).
2. NEW: `trees.catch_up(repo, task, milestone_branch)` — in the card's own worktree (`trees.card_tree(repo, task)`):
   a. REFUSE (today's message, verbatim) if the worktree directory does not exist — never conjure one — or if `git status --porcelain` is non-empty: A DIRTY TREE IS NEVER TOUCHED, somebody may be mid-thought in it even though the card is done.
   b. `git merge --no-edit <milestone_branch>` in that worktree, through `gitwork/run.py` like every git call.
   c. Clean → return the merge sha; `gitmoves.merge` proceeds into `trees.merge_card` exactly as if the card had never been behind.
   d. Conflict → `git merge --abort`, then raise a refusal that carries BOTH truths: the old cause ("N commits behind") AND git's own conflict words (the file list), plus the manual command — because now the human genuinely is the only one who can decide. Assert with a test that after the abort the worktree has no `MERGE_HEAD` and `status --porcelain` is empty.

WHY THIS DOES NOT VIOLATE "the worker's branch is the worker's": catch-up runs on ONE path only — a card whose state is `done`, inside the integration flow the orchestrator already invoked. The worker handed the card in; integrating it, including the mechanical half of integrating it, is the orchestrator's move and always was. A clean merge decides nothing — it executes the inevitable. State this in the docstring, because the next reader will ask.

TESTS in `tests/test_mcp.py`, next to the existing merge tests: (1) done card, branch behind by a clean commit → ONE `taskops_merge task=` integrates it, the ms branch contains both the catch-up and the `--no-ff` integration merge, the board records `merged`; (2) behind with a real conflict (both branches edit the same line) → refusal contains git's conflict file, the worktree is aborted-clean; (3) dirty worktree → today's refusal verbatim, nothing touched, `status --porcelain` unchanged; (4) missing worktree dir → refusal, no directory created. Mutation-check each guard one at a time — the dirty-tree guard especially: delete it and prove exactly one test goes red.

criteria: WHEN tasks=[…] is given, THE cards SHALL integrate in order through the single-card path and the answer SHALL report per card
WHEN done=true is given, THE server SHALL resolve the MERGE group itself and integrate it
WHEN a card fails, THE batch SHALL stop there, report the refusal verbatim, mark the rest not-reached, and a re-run SHALL continue
WHEN the MERGE group is empty, THE answer SHALL say so and error on nothing
card.spec:
THE COST, measured: the keys chapter integrated six cards — six separate `taskops_merge task=` calls, each preceded by the orchestrator noticing a done-notification, each a full round trip. The cards were sequential but even the parallel chapters (Monitor: 8 cards) paid one round trip per card. The board's own attention grouping says `MERGE — done, not integrated → taskops_merge` and then makes the orchestrator say it N times.

THE FIX, two spellings of one batch, both in `gitmoves.py::merge` beside the existing `task=` / `milestone=` split (the tool schema is `mcp/tools.py` — `taskops_merge` gains `tasks=[…]` and `done=true`; the wording of the tool description changes with it):

· `taskops_merge tasks=[tk-a, tk-b, tk-c]` — integrate exactly these, in the order given, each through the SINGLE-CARD PATH (including card 1's catch-up — this card adds no second merge implementation, it LOOPS the first; state that in the docstring, it is the whole design).
· `taskops_merge done=true` — resolve the list server-side: every card the board currently groups under MERGE (`verbs/pulse.py::run` — done, `merged_into` empty), in the group's own order, then the same loop.

STOP AT THE FIRST FAILURE, whatever its kind — conflict, dirty tree, refusal — and REPORT EVERYTHING: per card, `merged <sha>` | `stopped: <the refusal, verbatim>` | `not reached`. Partial completion is not rollback-able and must not pretend to be: each successful merge is a real `--no-ff` commit and a real `merged` event, both idempotent to re-run (`taskops_merge done=true` again continues where it stopped — pin THAT with a test, it is the property that makes stopping safe).

WHAT THIS IS NOT: auto-integration on done. The orchestrator still calls it — review-gated chapters still see verdicts first, and integrating remains a decision. What dies is only the N-fold repetition of the decision already taken.

TESTS: (1) three done cards, one behind-but-clean → one call, three merges, three `merged` events, per-card report; (2) second of three conflicts → first merged, second stopped with the refusal verbatim, third `not reached`, and a re-run after fixing continues from the second; (3) `done=true` with an empty MERGE group answers honestly ("nothing to integrate") rather than erroring; (4) `tasks=[]` is a BadRequest naming both spellings. Mutation-check the stop-at-first logic: make it continue past a failure and prove exactly the not-reached test goes red.

criteria: WHEN two ready cards declare disjoint files and share no spec terms, THE wave SHALL list both as safe
WHEN two ready cards share a file or a concept term, THE held entry SHALL name the other card and the exact overlap
WHEN an assign names cards the wave holds apart, THE briefs SHALL carry the warning and the assign SHALL still proceed
WHEN the board has one or zero ready cards, THE payload SHALL carry wave: null
WHEN a spec contains only ordinary prose, THE term extraction SHALL yield nothing
card.spec:
THE COST, quoted from this repo's own post-mortems, because it is the most-repeated failure of the whole project: two `ago()`, three `initials()`, two `gitwork/remote.py` (same path, complementary halves — "because both their specs said check `git remote get-url origin`"), two smoke sections both numbered §9, and two `const reviewed` in one scope. `docs/fan-out.md`'s conclusion — a CONCEPT named by two cards is a seam; land it serialized first — is a sentence in `mcp/server.py::INSTRUCTIONS` that the orchestrator must remember at dispatch time. Twice this week it was not remembered, because nothing on the board computes it.

Meanwhile `collisions()` (`verbs/_context.py`) already warns on overlapping declared FILES — but per-take, after dispatch, one card at a time. The moment that decides parallelism is EARLIER: the orchestrator looking at the ready column deciding what to fan out.

THE FIX, three layers, all derived, all advisory:

1. `core/seams.py` — NEW, PURE (level 1: no I/O, no clock). Two functions:
   · `terms(spec: str) -> frozenset[str]`: the CONCEPT-BEARING tokens of a spec's prose — backticked spans and path-shaped/dotted/underscored identifiers (`git remote get-url origin`, `panels.ts::WorktreeRow`, `live.renew`), lowercased, length ≥ 4. NOT ordinary words: the extraction is deliberately narrow, because a false wave-hold teaches the orchestrator to ignore the wave. Document the grammar in the docstring with the real examples above.
   · `overlaps(cards: {id: spec}) -> list[(id, id, shared_terms)]`: pairwise shared terms among the given specs, empty-set pairs dropped.
2. `verbs/pulse.py::run` — the payload gains `wave`, computed ONLY over `groups.take` (ready cards; a board with ≤1 ready card sends `wave: null` and spends nothing): partition the ready cards into (a) `safe`: the largest prefix-greedy set whose declared `files` are pairwise disjoint AND whose specs share no terms, in the group's own priority order; (b) `held`: the rest, each with `why` — `{"with": tk-x, "files": […]}` or `{"with": tk-x, "terms": […]}`. Greedy-by-priority is deliberately simple and stated: an optimal partition is NP-shaped and the answer is advice, not truth.
3. THE SURFACES: `mcp/render.py` — the board tool's MERGE…TAKE listing draws the wave under TAKE ("▸ safe to dispatch together: tk-a tk-b tk-c · held: tk-d (names `remote get-url` with tk-a)"); `mcp/brief.py` / `gitmoves.assign` — when an assign call names cards the wave holds APART, the brief's header carries the warning sentence (assign still proceeds — rule 1, never a lock).

UI: NOT in this card. The payload key is there for a future pane; `ui/src/types.ts` gets the OPTIONAL type with its @source line and nothing draws it yet — say so in the close note.

TESTS: `tests/test_verbs.py` for `seams.terms` (each documented example extracts; ordinary prose extracts nothing — pin "the board refuses" yielding ∅) and the wave partition (disjoint → all safe; shared file → held names the file; shared term → held names the term; one ready card → null). `tests/test_mcp.py`: the render line, and the assign warning appearing ONLY when the wave holds the pair apart. Mutation-check: widen `terms` to ordinary words and prove the false-positive test goes red.
card.title: The wave: which ready cards are safe to dispatch together, and why the rest wait

criteria: WHEN a finished chapter is behind a moved trunk and the merge is clean, THE landing call SHALL catch up and land in one step
WHEN the catch-up conflicts, THE refusal SHALL name the files and master SHALL be untouched, exactly as today
WHEN the chapter's criteria are unanswered, THE criteria refusal SHALL come before any git runs
WHEN card 1 and this card both exist, THE catch-up SHALL be one shared function in trees.py
card.spec:
THE COST, reproduced twice in two days, verbatim from the second time:

    ✗ ms/the-server-becomes-v2-taskops-be conflicts with master in:
      ARCHITECTURE.md
      CLAUDE.md
      (merge aborted — master is untouched)

WHY IT HAPPENS BY CONSTRUCTION: a chapter's branch is cut at its first `taskops_assign` (`gitwork/trees.py::ensure_card` → `ensure_milestone`) from the trunk AS OF THAT MOMENT. Chapters overlap — while one is in flight another lands — so by landing time the trunk has moved, and the docs both chapters legitimately touched (CLAUDE.md's counts, ARCHITECTURE's status) collide. Both times the human's fix was mechanical: `git merge master` in the integration worktree (`.taskops/trees/_ms-<slug>/`), resolve-or-not, land again. The FIRST time it was even clean — pure count drift — and still cost a manual round trip.

THE FIX mirrors card 1 exactly, one level up, at `gitmoves.py::_land` before `trees.land_milestone`:

1. NEW `trees.behind_trunk(repo, milestone_branch)` — the same `merge-base --is-ancestor` + `rev-list --count` shape as `behind()`, against `base_ref(repo)` (the function that already knows what the trunk is; the UI chapter's "the trunk the UI does not know" reasoning says why nothing else may guess it).
2. Behind and the integration worktree is CLEAN → `git merge --no-edit <trunk>` there. Clean merge → proceed into `land_milestone` unchanged. Conflict → abort and raise EXACTLY today's refusal (the one quoted above — it is good: it names the files and guarantees master untouched) with the behind-count added.
3. Dirty integration worktree → today's behaviour, untouched.

SHARE THE MECHANISM WITH CARD 1, do not duplicate it: `catch_up(repo, worktree_dir, onto_branch)` should be ONE function in `trees.py` that both call sites use — a card catching up to its chapter and a chapter catching up to the trunk are the same act on different pairs. If card 1 shipped it with a card-specific signature, generalise it here and keep card 1's tests green unchanged; two near-identical catch-ups would be this chapter committing the exact sin its wave-card exists to warn about.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: the landing GATE itself — open work refuses, criteria_met refuses, the human's answer is still required BEFORE any git runs (the catch-up included: no criteria answer, no touch). Order in `_land`: gate checks first, catch-up second, land third.

TESTS: (1) chapter behind master by a clean docs commit → ONE `taskops_merge milestone= criteria_met=true` lands it, master's history shows catch-up + landing; (2) the ARCHITECTURE/CLAUDE two-sided edit → refusal with the file list, master byte-identical before/after (pin with rev-parse); (3) criteria unanswered + behind → the criteria refusal comes FIRST and no merge ran (assert the integration worktree's HEAD unmoved); (4) not behind → today's path byte-for-byte. Mutation-check the ordering of gate-before-catch-up: swap them and prove test 3 goes red.

criteria: WHEN two branches each add one section file and merge, THE merge SHALL produce zero conflicts and both sections SHALL run
WHEN the sections are migrated, THE assertion bodies SHALL be byte-identical — movement, not rewriting
WHEN run.mjs builds, THE generated index SHALL be deterministic by filename and SHALL NOT be committed
WHEN two section files claim one slug, THE generator SHALL refuse loudly
WHEN npm run check runs, THE four steps SHALL be green including the git diff clause
card.spec:
THE COST, four real incidents in two days, all in ONE file. `ui/smoke/main.tsx` (~2.300 lines) is an appendix every UI card APPENDS a section to — which makes every pair of parallel UI cards conflict BY CONSTRUCTION, exactly like the committed bundle before `.gitattributes -merge`, except text-mergeable enough that git sometimes "succeeds" and produces garbage:

  · tk-a1b7f2 × tk-63f919: both appended at the tail → a 293-line conflict block the orchestrator resolved by hand;
  · the same merge auto-stacked TWO `const reviewed` declarations in one scope — caught only by tsc, i.e. the "success" case was the dangerous one;
  · two waves earlier, two workers each created a section numbered §9 — the numbering itself is append-order state;
  · the docs audit found every `ui/smoke/main.tsx §N` cross-reference dangling, because the numbers moved as sections were inserted.

THE FIX — the repo's own shape, not a tool change: sections become FILES.

1. `ui/smoke/sections/<slug>.tsx` — one file per section, named by what it pins (`worktrees-index.tsx`, `closing-note.tsx`, … — slugs, NEVER numbers: the §-numbering was the collision), each exporting `run(fixture, check, harness)` with the signature the existing sections de-facto share; extract it as a declared type in a `sections/section.ts` seam — this is `panels.ts`'s move, the one docs/fan-out.md prescribes, applied to the harness.
2. `ui/smoke/main.tsx` shrinks to the shared plumbing (fixture load, `check`, the harness helpers) plus the section DISCOVERY. esbuild needs static imports, so the index of sections is GENERATED: `run.mjs`, which already builds `main.tsx` through esbuild before running it, gains a pre-step that `readdir`s `sections/`, writes `sections/index.generated.ts` (imports in FILENAME order — deterministic, so the run order is stable and no file 'goes first' by merge accident), and the generated file is gitignored — never committed, never mergeable, never a conflict.
3. MIGRATE the existing ~11 sections mechanically — cut at the existing `/* ── N. title */` banners, one file each, ZERO assertion bodies edited (this card must be reviewable as pure movement; `git log --follow` should still work). The section-local `const`s that collided (`reviewed`, `handedBoard`) become file-local by construction — which is the entire point.
4. `tests/test_ui.py` keeps working unchanged IF it only shells out to `run.mjs` — verify; if it imports main.tsx paths, adjust minimally. The marker tuples in `test_ui.py` stay as they are: they are single-line appends whose conflicts are trivial, and moving them is scope creep.
5. Rebuild the committed bundle ONCE if `src/main.tsx` was touched (it should NOT be — the smoke harness is not bundled; assert that with `git diff` and say so), and run the full closure: `cd ui && npm run check`, all four steps green.

THE ACCEPTANCE that matters is the parallel one, and it must be TESTED as such: in a throwaway clone inside the test (or a scripted check), create two branches off the result, each adding a new section file + nothing else, merge both — zero conflicts, both sections run. That is the property the whole card buys; without it pinned, the next refactor quietly reintroduces the appendix.

Mutation-check the discovery: delete one section file and prove the smoke count drops and `run.mjs` still exits by its own rules; shadow two sections with the same slug and prove the generator refuses (two files, one name, is the §9 bug reborn — refuse it loudly).

criteria: A done card whose branch is behind its chapter integrates in ONE taskops_merge call when the merge is clean — no human runs git — and a conflicted one refuses with git's words and an aborted-clean worktree.
One call integrates every done card of a chapter, in order, reporting per card, stopping at the first conflict.
The board names the dispatch-safe wave among ready cards and says WHY each excluded card is held — and nothing is blocked by it.
A chapter landing over a moved trunk catches up automatically when clean; the two-days-ago ARCHITECTURE/CLAUDE conflict scenario still aborts with master untouched.
Two UI cards adding smoke coverage in parallel touch zero shared lines in ui/smoke/.
body.goal: Two days of running this board at full tilt — 16 chapters, 100+ cards, up to 8 workers in parallel — produced a measured conclusion: the workers were never the bottleneck, the ORCHESTRATOR's serial toil was. ~9 stale-branch refusals executed by hand, every integration a separate round trip, two chapters landing into conflict because the trunk moved underneath them, and every pair of parallel UI cards colliding in one appendix file. Each cost is reproduced, quoted, and killed in this chapter — by mechanism, never by a lock: warnings stay warnings, a conflict still stops everything, and no rule from ARCHITECTURE.md §11 bends.
rules: A WARNING IS NEVER A LOCK. The wave, the concept overlaps, the collision notes — all advisory, exactly like `collisions()` today. The board informs; the orchestrator decides. Anything that blocks a dispatch because prose looked similar is refused on sight.

AUTO-MERGE ONLY WHEN GIT SAYS CLEAN, AND ONLY ON PATHS THAT ALREADY BELONG TO INTEGRATION. A conflict aborts and reports with git's own words, leaving the tree exactly as the abort leaves it — the current behaviour. A dirty worktree is never touched. The worker's branch stays the worker's: catch-up runs only on a DONE card already being integrated, which is the one moment its branch is the board's business.
NOTHING NEW IS STORED. The wave, the overlaps, the batch results — all derived per read from state the board already holds. No new event kind, no new sqlite table, no cache of an analysis.
taskops NEVER PARSES SOURCE CODE. The concept-overlap warning reads SPECS — prose the planner wrote — never the repo's files. That line is docs/fan-out.md's conclusion and it does not move.

Every card quotes its reproduction from this board's own history and pins the fix with a test that fails first. Mutation-check one site at a time; commit first; restore with `git checkout -- <file>` — `cp` is aliased to `cp -i` here.

This chapter brings back the CONVENIENCE without those three costs: GitHub proves WHO you are once, the server enrols your key from it, and from that moment on the ordinary ssh-key session is what every call uses. GitHub is the introduction, never the credential.
rules: The GitHub token is used for ONE call, server-side, and is never stored — not in the log, not in server.sqlite, not in remote.json. What persists is the enrolled pubkey, exactly as an invite leaves.
After enrolment nothing changes: every later call is the same signed ssh session. There is no second credential type and no second door in `scope.permit`.
Zero runtime dependencies stays true: stdlib urllib through _wire.py, no requests, no PyGithub.
A board must OPT IN by naming its repo (owner/name) and the access level required; a board that names none keeps working exactly as today, invite-only.
GitHub being unreachable must refuse loudly and never fall back to granting access.
body.title: GitHub membership opens a board

card.spec: A board-level fact, through `verbs/project.py`'s existing op table (that file already owns board facts: op=remote, op=visibility): op=forge with {host: github, repo: owner/name, need: push|admin}. Recorded by the OWNER only, derived per read like visibility, absent by default. `gitwork/remote.py::remember` already parses an origin into {host, slug, url} — reuse it rather than a second parser, and refuse a repo that is not owner/name. This lands FIRST and alone: the login card and the CLI card both read this vocabulary.
card.title: The board declares its forge repo and the access it requires (THE SEAM)

card.spec: A door beside `/login`: the caller sends {github_token, principal, pubkey}; the server asks GitHub ONCE (GET /repos/{owner}/{name} with that token, read `permissions.push`) through `_wire.py` — stdlib only — and on push=true enrols the pubkey exactly as `invite/redeem` does (`store/pubkeys.py` + allowed_signers rewritten whole). The token is never written anywhere: not logged, not stored, not echoed in the answer. `http/login.py` owns this because it owns enrolment; `core/scope.py` gates it with the same `permit` table. Refusals: no forge declared on this board · GitHub unreachable (loud, never a grant) · push=false, naming the repo and the level that would work. Rate/abuse note: an unauthenticated GitHub call is 60/h, an authenticated one 5000 — this is authenticated by the caller's own token, so the budget is theirs.
card.title: The host verifies GitHub membership and enrols the key — one call, nothing stored

card.spec: `--github` takes the token from `gh auth token` (the CLI everyone already has) or `$GITHUB_TOKEN`, else prompts hidden; never from a flag value, so it cannot land in shell history. It sends token+pubkey to the door above, and on success the key signs in ON THE SPOT — the same `identity.establish` path a `--invite` join takes, so what lands in remote.json is a SESSION with an expiry and a login block, never the GitHub token. One refusal per failure mode, each naming the way out. `taskops join <board>` bare keeps working unchanged for an already-enrolled key.
card.title: taskops join <board> --github — the whole flow in one command

card.spec: ARCHITECTURE gains the section: why GitHub is an INTRODUCTION and not a credential, the three costs v1 paid that this avoids, and where the token does not go. README gains `--github` beside `--invite` in the join flows. taskops-v2's CLAUDE.md tool/flag surface updated. Then the payoff: `~/axion-v3/README.md` currently says GitHub membership does NOT yet grant board access — replace that note with the real steps, and declare the forge on the axion board (op=forge, cloudacio/Axion, need=push) so JP's onboarding becomes one command with no invite.

criteria: `taskops board pull <name>` materialises the hosted history locally, proves every event id arrived, flips the config last, and leaves the host untouched — verified by reading the host after.
An interrupted pull re-runs to a no-op and never leaves a checkout half-pointed at two boards.

body.goal:
A board's life is one-directional today: `board create` makes one and `board push` promotes a local history into it, but nothing brings a board back down and NOTHING takes one off a host. So a board is created from the laptop and can only be removed by ssh-ing to the box and deleting a directory — which contradicts the design's own line, that after the bootstrap nothing on a host is ever administered over a shell. Worse, that deletion is unguarded: `rm -rf` on a board directory destroys the only copy of a history nobody can regenerate.

This chapter closes the loop with the guardrail FIRST. `board pull` is `board push` run backwards, with the same discipline: stream the whole history down, VERIFY it arrived event for event, and only then flip the config — and the host keeps everything, so a pull destroys nothing. `board rm` then refuses to take a board down whose history this checkout does not already hold, naming both ways out exactly as `join` refuses to orphan a local board. Destroying history stays possible, because a system whose only door is its own API cannot be repaired when that API is what broke — but it becomes a sentence somebody typed on purpose, never a side effect.
rules: A pull DESTROYS NOTHING: the host keeps its board, byte for byte. Only this checkout's config changes, and only after the history verified.

Verification is by EVENT ID, never by a count and never by an exit code — the same rule `board push` already holds itself to. A pull that cannot prove every id arrived must refuse and leave the config untouched.

`board rm` refuses by default and names BOTH ways out, the way `join`'s orphan refusal does. Destroying history takes a flag somebody typed on purpose; it is never the default and never a side effect of anything else.

No new replication: pulling uses the `events` verb that already pages the log. Nothing syncs, nothing is kept in step, and a pulled board is a SNAPSHOT that stops moving — say so where a human reads it.
Removing a board is OWNER-only server scope, like `board.visibility` — same table, same role gate, no second door in `core/scope.py`.
body.title: The lifecycle runs backwards too — pull, and a board that cannot be lost

card.spec:
A pure comparison in `core/`, consumed by BOTH halves so they cannot disagree about what 'safe' means: given the ids a host reports and the ids a local board holds, answer whether the local copy is complete, and name what is missing when it is not. This is what `board pull` asserts before flipping the config AND what `board rm` demands before destroying anything — one function, two callers, exactly like `core/reports.py::under` guards the write and the read.

It takes SETS OF IDS, not counts: `board push` already learned that a count agreeing proves nothing about WHICH events arrived (its docstring carries that post-mortem — read it before designing this). Return enough for a refusal to be actionable: how many are missing and a couple of examples, never a bare boolean.

Lands first and alone: the pull card and the rm card both consume this vocabulary, and a concept named by two cards is a seam.
card.title: THE SEAM — 'is this history held here?', the one question both new verbs ask

card.spec:
`taskops board pull [<name>]` brings a hosted board down to this checkout. The name defaults exactly as every other board verb's does (recorded name, else the directory); `<host>/<name>` is the explicit form.

The ORDER is the safety, and it is `cli/push.py`'s order reversed — read that module first, it argues every step:
1. Refuse if this checkout already holds a LOCAL board with events (the `join` guardrail, same sentence family: it would be orphaned).
2. Page the whole log down through the `events` verb — no new server verb, no replication channel.
3. Write it through `Stores.write` so the journal→index→fold order is the store's, never a hand-rolled file copy.
4. VERIFY with the seam card's comparison, by id.
5. ONLY THEN flip `board.json` to a local board, and keep `remote.json`'s login block — the host is still where `board create`/`push` would go.
An interrupted run re-runs to a no-op.

Say in the output what a pulled board IS: a snapshot that stops moving. Nothing syncs afterwards, and a reader who thinks otherwise will be wrong for days without noticing.
card.title: taskops board pull — board push, run backwards, and the host keeps everything

card.spec:
A `board.remove` admin verb (server scope, OWNER only, beside `board.visibility` in `http/admin.py::REGISTRY` — copy its shape end to end) plus `taskops board rm <name>` in the CLI.

THE GUARDRAIL IS THE CARD. By default it REFUSES unless this checkout already holds the board's history, asked through the seam card's comparison against the host's real ids — not against a local guess. The refusal names both ways out, exactly as `commands.py::ORPHAN` does for join:
    taskops board pull <name>          take the history down first, then remove
    taskops board rm <name> --discard-history    destroy it anyway; say so out loud
The flag's name is the point: `--force` is banned in this project (ARCHITECTURE §11) because it says nothing about what it overrides. This one names the thing being destroyed.

body.reason:
`taskops board pull [<name>]` lands in 86c535b — push's five steps reversed, config flipping LAST.

WHAT IT IS: new `cli/pull.py` (198 lines) + `cli/paging.py::whole_log` (the transport: pages a board's whole log down through the existing `events` verb, keyset by seq, verifying each event's id against its own content on arrival, returns oldest-first + the `total` the host claims). `main.py` routes `pull` beside `push`. Two small shared seams: `core/event.of` (the ONE coercion, split out of `from_line` so a caller holding a parsed OBJECT reaches it without re-serialising a dict to have it parsed back) and `gitwork/install.write_local` (board.json → `{}`, remote.json untouched — now shared with `taskops init`, which had the same two lines inline).

THE ORDER, and the two decisions that are not obvious:
1. Step 1 is judged BY ID, not by existence. "Is there a local board here" is the obvious guard and it is the WRONG one: a pull that died after step 3 leaves exactly that, so the retry would refuse itself and the checkout would be stranded between two boards with no command able to finish the job. What must be refused is a local history the HOST DOES NOT HOLD (it really would be merged — two histories in one log), so `holding.compare` decides and a partial copy of the board being pulled is recognised as the resumed pull it is. Refusal names both ways out, `join`-orphan style: `join --discard-local` then pull, or pull in a checkout with no local board.
2. TWO checks, neither substituting for the other: `total` guards the PAGING (a page silently lost shrinks both sides of an id comparison and agrees with itself → MOVED refusal), the ID SET guards the WRITE (`holding.compare` by id → SHORT refusal). Step 3 writes only what is not already held, because the cache ignores a repeated id and the log does not.

A PULLED BOARD IS A SNAPSHOT THAT STOPS MOVING — nothing syncs afterwards. Printed by the command itself, every time, and in README.

PROOF, real socket, real keypair, output of `main(["board","pull",…])`:
  reading http://127.0.0.1:50292/facturador …
    4 new event(s) written · all 4 event(s) are held here
  …/mine/.taskops/board.json now reads the local copy in …/mine/.taskops/board
    http://127.0.0.1:50292/facturador still holds every one of those events — a pull destroys nothing,
    and remote.json keeps its login: board create / board push still go there.
    This copy is a SNAPSHOT and it STOPS MOVING: nothing syncs from here on, so
    anything done on http://…/facturador after this second will never appear in it.

WHAT PINS IT — ten tests, one contiguous block at the END of tests/test_topology.py: comes_down_whole_and_the_host_keeps_every_byte (host log read back byte for byte after the pull, ids equal, board.json local, remote.json still holds login+token) · is_a_SNAPSHOT_and_it_stops_moving (the wording AND the fact: the host plans a second chapter, the local copy still sees one) · an_interrupted_pull_re_runs_to_a_no_op (Stores.write dies mid-write → half a history and a config that never flipped; the retry finishes it with no duplicate line; a THIRD run is byte-identical on both sides) · over_a_history_the_host_does_not_hold_names_both_ways_out · arrives_short_stops_before_the_config_flips · moved_under_the_read · page_by_page (MAX_PAGE shrunk to 2) · fails_its_own_hash_is_never_written_down · pulling_added_no_verb_to_either_registry (`board.pull` is not a verb this host answers).

body.text:
STOP — the ground moved under this card. I killed jp1 mid-work on purpose, because it was about to write an onboarding README naming a host the axion board no longer lives on.

The axion board MOVED, tonight, at Berna's request (the home box was too slow):

  from  https://taskops.bernardocastro.dev/axion   (nginx on the GCP relay → proxy_pass 10.8.0.2 → LXD container on the home box)
  to    https://boards.t.bernardocastro.dev/axion  (taskops 0.3.1 SERVED BY the GCP relay itself, systemd unit `taskops`, 127.0.0.1:8787 behind nginx)

Measured, which is why it moved: /healthz is 0.36s on the new host against 0.77s on the old one — the relay→box hop was 178ms each way.

How it moved, and what survives:
- `board pull axion` brought 962 events down ("all 962 event(s) are held here"), then `board create` + `board push axion` on the new host: "verified: 962 landed, seq 963".
- The OLD host still holds its copy — a pull destroys nothing. Nobody has removed it, and that is Berna's call, not this card's.
- jp1's work was NOT wasted: it declared the forge before it was stopped (event 925540b6…, ts 1786393854, `{op: forge, repo: cloudacio/Axion, need: push}`), and that event travelled with the 962. The GitHub door is live on the new host — `POST /axion/join/github` answers 400 with the body shape it wants, no longer 409 "opened by invite".

So for whoever picks this up: every URL in the README is `boards.t.bernardocastro.dev`, the forge step is already done and must not be re-declared, and the milestone's rule still holds — every command in the README gets run at least once, and you say plainly which ones you could not run because you are the owner and not JP.

One papercut found while doing this, worth its own card and NOT this one: bare `taskops board pull` in a joined checkout defaults the board name to the DIRECTORY (`axion-v3`) instead of the board `board.json` names (`axion`), so it refused with "no board named 'axion-v3'". `board pull axion` works.
